pages.title: LIRA
pages.for: Condition and place, from one end. It finds the length, the joints, and water or damage along the cable. At commissioning, it sets the baseline for later years.

pages.html: Negative points to water getting in, heat damage or mechanical damage. Positive points to bends and breaks in the shield. Red means significant, amber intermediate and green mild.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
LIRA sends a sweep of small sine waves into one pair of conductors at one end. It records the cable's impedance at each frequency. From that record, it finds where the impedance changes between any two metal conductors. That can be a core and its screen, two cores, or a core and the armour. It gives the length, the joints, and where water or dirt has got in. Each wave runs to the far end and back to the set. So it needs only one end.

It is used around loadout, during installation, at commissioning, and in service at set intervals. The commissioning record is the cable's baseline. LIRA gives no pass or fail. You compare each test with the baseline. So always keep the raw trace data.

Some systems also monitor energised cables, up to 33 kV, through sensors that do not touch the core. String B runs at 66 kV, above that. So it is tested dead. Both ends are earthed and discharged first, so no energy is stored in the cable.

If it is skipped

Skip it, and there is no baseline to compare with in later years. And L2's fault rests on one test, from one end.

pages.name: The why: the cable rings
pages.text: Take one core and its screen, with the far end open. At low frequency the pair is just a capacitor. Its reactance is 1 ÷ 2πfC. It starts high and falls as the frequency rises. As the frequency climbs, each wave reaches the far end and comes back. Where a quarter wavelength fits the cable, the trip there and back is half a wavelength. So it comes back upside down and cancels the wave going in. At the test end, the cable looks like a short, and the impedance dips. Where half a wavelength fits, the round trip is a whole wavelength. The wave arrives back in step. The cable looks like an open, and the impedance peaks. Each extra half wavelength repeats the pattern. So the dips come every v ÷ 2L, where v is the velocity and L the length. A longer cable fits more half wavelengths into the same band. So its resonances crowd together. This record of impedance against frequency is the cable's impedance spectrum. An end matched exactly to the cable soaks up every wave, so nothing comes back and there are no resonances. At 2.40 km the dips sit 35.0 kHz apart. The first is at 17.5 kHz. At 1.20 km they spread to 70.0 kHz apart. At 4.80 km they crowd to 17.5 kHz. With the end matched, no wave comes back. So the line goes flat at 27.1 Ω.
pages.alt: Take one core and its screen, with the far end open. At low frequency the pair is just a capacitor. Its reactance is 1 ÷ 2πfC. It starts high and falls as the frequency rises. As the frequency climbs, each wave reaches the far end and comes back. Where a quarter wavelength fits the cable, the trip there and back is half a wavelength. So it comes back upside down and cancels the wave going in. At the test end, the cable looks like a short, and the impedance dips. Where half a wavelength fits, the round trip is a whole wavelength. The wave arrives back in step.

pages.name: The why: a change becomes a spot
pages.text: Now give the core a short length of damaged insulation. Water raises the permittivity, so the capacitance there rises. The impedance is the square root of L ÷ C per metre. So it falls. A little of each wave reflects from that spot, as a TDR pulse does. Call the spot's distance x. The echo comes back after a round trip of 2x ÷ v. The echo is late. So it slips in and out of step with the main signal as the frequency rises. In step, it adds. Out of step, it takes away. So it puts a small ripple on the spectrum. It comes back in step each time the frequency rises by 1 ÷ round trip. That is v ÷ 2x. So a nearer spot makes a wider ripple. LIRA's software turns each ripple back into a round trip. Then it turns each round trip into a place with the TDR rule again, L = t × v ÷ 2. The result is the spot signature. It lays the cable out by distance, with its end, its joints and any spots. The software works on the phase of the impedance. The phase can show small changes better. Each spot is graded by DNORM. Its sign follows the type of change. Negative means water, heat or mechanical damage. Positive means bends and shield breaks. Its colour gives the severity. Green is mild, amber intermediate and red significant. The bands here are practice values. On a real job they are a software or client setting. At 961 m the round trip is 11.44 µs. That is close to TDR's 11.43 µs. The ripple repeats every 87.4 kHz. At 100 m the arrow is short. The ripple is wide, every 840.0 kHz. At 2300 m it tightens to every 36.5 kHz. The spot follows the change along the cable. Switched to a shield break, the bar flips above the line in the same place.
pages.alt: Then switch its type. Its echo comes back after 11.44 µs, so the ripple repeats every 87.4 kHz.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: Take these practice values. LIRA runs from the OSS on L2. The software finds a ripple that repeats every 87.4 kHz. Where is the change that makes it? A ripple every 87.4 kHz means an echo with a round trip of 11.44 µs. At 168.0 m/µs, that is 11.44 × 168.0 ÷ 2 = 961.0 m from the OSS. That is within 0.9 m of TDR's 960.1 m.
pages.alt: 1 Set up on the dead cable, earthed and discharged at both ends. Connect the leads core to screen, as the test specification says, with the earths still on. Then lift L2's earth at your end under control. The B01 technician lifts L2's earth there, so its far end is open. 2 The rule: a ripple that repeats every Δ in frequency comes from an echo with a round trip of 1 ÷ Δ. 3 t = 1 ÷ 87 400 Hz = 11.44 µs. 4 Then the TDR rule: L = t × v ÷ 2. 5 L = 11.44 × 168.0 ÷ 2 = 961.0 m from the OSS. 6 TDR put the fault at 960.1 m. The two agree within 0.9 m.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain what LIRA measures, and why it needs only one end.
pages.why: A model answer: LIRA measures where the impedance changes between two metal conductors, such as a core and its screen. It sweeps many frequencies into the pair and records the impedance at each. With the far end not matched, the cable resonates at frequencies set by its length and velocity. Water or damage changes the insulation's permittivity. That changes the impedance at that spot and adds a ripple to the spectrum. Each wave travels to the far end and reflects back to the end it was sent from. So the set needs only one end. In practice it is still tested from both ends, for the best sensitivity and to confirm where a spot is.

Gentle, low-voltage checks come first. The withstand test, which can break a weak cable down, comes near the end. The LIRA baseline comes last, so it records each healthy core as it goes into service. On a real job you would stop and report after the sheath failed. Here the VLF test ran anyway, so one fault shows in five tests.
